2-1.title: Commas in a Series
2-1.learn:
HOW TO USE COMMAS IN A SERIES

When you list THREE or more items, separate each item with a comma. The comma before the final 'and' is called the Oxford comma, and it keeps the last two items from blurring together.

Example 1 — 'I packed apples, sandwiches, and water.'
Three items: apples / sandwiches / water. Commas go after 'apples' and 'sandwiches,' including before 'and.'

Example 2 — 'We visited Miami, Orlando, and Tampa.'
Three cities are listed, so a comma separates each one, including before the final 'and.'

Example 3 — Why the last comma matters: 'I love my parents, Beyonce and Jay-Z' could sound like your parents ARE Beyonce and Jay-Z. With the series comma — 'I love my parents, Beyonce, and Jay-Z' — it is clearly a list of four things.

Remember: only use series commas when there are THREE or more items. For just two items joined by 'and' (apples and water), no comma is needed.

questions.question: Which sentence uses series commas CORRECTLY?

choices.A: I bought milk eggs and bread.
choices.B: I bought milk, eggs, and bread.
choices.C: I bought, milk eggs, and bread.
choices.D: I bought milk, eggs and, bread.

questions.explanation: Three items in a list each get a comma, including before the final 'and.'

questions.question: Which list is punctuated correctly?

choices.B: red white and blue
choices.D: red white, and, blue

questions.explanation: Commas separate each of the three colors, with a comma before 'and.'

questions.question: How many commas are needed in this list of FOUR items: 'apples oranges grapes and pears'?

choices.B: Two
choices.D: Four

questions.explanation: Four items need three commas: 'apples, oranges, grapes, and pears.'

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: She plays soccer basketball and tennis.
choices.B: She plays soccer, basketball, and tennis.
choices.C: She plays, soccer basketball and tennis.
choices.D: She plays soccer, basketball and, tennis.

questions.explanation: The three sports each get a comma, including before the final 'and.'

questions.question: Which sentence does NOT need any series commas?

choices.A: We saw lions, tigers, and bears.
choices.B: We saw lions and tigers.
choices.C: We packed shirts, pants, and socks.
choices.D: He likes math, science, and art.

questions.explanation: Only two items joined by 'and' do not need a comma; a series comma is for three or more items.

questions.question: Where do the commas belong: 'The flag is red white and blue'?

choices.A: The flag is red, white and blue
choices.B: The flag is, red white, and blue
choices.C: The flag is red, white, and blue
choices.D: The flag, is red white and blue

questions.explanation: Each of the three colors is separated by a comma, including before 'and.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly lists actions in a series?

choices.B: He ran, jumped, and swam.
choices.D: He, ran jumped, and swam.

questions.explanation: The three verbs each get a comma, including before the final 'and.'

questions.question: Why does the series comma help in 'I invited my friends, the principal, and the coach'?

choices.A: It makes clear the friends are separate from the principal and coach.
choices.B: It adds extra people to the list.
choices.C: It is only there for decoration.
choices.D: It changes the meaning to one person.

questions.explanation: Without the series comma, it could read as if the friends ARE the principal and coach; the comma keeps them separate.

questions.question: Which sentence has a comma error in the series?

choices.A: We need pens, paper, and folders.
choices.B: We need pens paper, and folders.
choices.C: We need pens, paper, glue, and tape.
choices.D: We need rulers, scissors, and markers.

questions.explanation: Choice B is missing the comma after 'pens'; a series needs a comma between every item.

questions.question: Which list of FIVE items is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: north south east west and center
choices.B: north, south, east, west, and center
choices.C: north, south east, west and center
choices.D: north south, east west, and center

questions.explanation: Five items in a series need four commas, with one before the final 'and.'

2-2.title: Commas with Introductory Phrases
2-2.learn:
HOW TO USE A COMMA AFTER AN INTRODUCTORY ELEMENT

When a sentence opens with an introductory word, phrase, or clause before the main idea, put a comma right after it. The comma signals where the warm-up ends and the main idea begins.

Example 1 — 'After the storm, we cleaned the yard.'
'After the storm' is the introduction; the comma comes before the main idea, 'we cleaned the yard.'

Example 2 — 'Yes, I will help you.'
A single introductory word like 'Yes,' 'No,' or 'Well' is followed by a comma.

Example 3 — 'When the bell rang, the students left.'
'When the bell rang' is an introductory dependent clause, so a comma follows it before the main clause.

Tip: If the sentence starts with the SUBJECT first ('We cleaned the yard after the storm'), no introductory comma is needed. The comma is only for words that come BEFORE the main subject and verb.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated CORRECTLY?

choices.B: After lunch, we went outside.
choices.D: After lunch we, went outside.

questions.explanation: A comma follows the introductory phrase 'After lunch' before the main idea.

questions.question: Where does the comma belong: 'In the morning I brush my teeth'?

choices.A: In the morning, I brush my teeth
choices.B: In, the morning I brush my teeth
choices.C: In the morning I brush, my teeth
choices.D: In the, morning I brush my teeth

questions.explanation: The introductory phrase 'In the morning' is followed by a comma before the main clause.

questions.question: Which sentence needs a comma added after the introductory word?

choices.B: I agree with you.
choices.D: They agree too.

questions.explanation: The introductory word 'Yes' should be followed by a comma: 'Yes, I agree with you.'

questions.question: Which sentence does NOT need an introductory comma?

choices.B: We stretched before the game.
choices.D: When it rained we stayed in.

questions.explanation: Choice B starts with the subject 'We,' so no introductory comma is needed; the others begin with introductory elements.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates the introductory clause?

choices.A: Because she was late she missed the bus.
choices.B: Because she was late, she missed the bus.
choices.C: Because, she was late she missed the bus.
choices.D: Because she, was late she missed the bus.

questions.explanation: The introductory dependent clause 'Because she was late' is followed by a comma.

questions.question: Where should the comma go: 'Suddenly the lights went out'?

choices.B: Suddenly the lights, went out
choices.D: No comma is needed

questions.explanation: The introductory word 'Suddenly' is followed by a comma before the main idea.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the introductory comma correctly?

choices.A: During the long, boring movie I fell asleep.
choices.B: During the long, boring movie, I fell asleep.
choices.C: During, the long boring movie I fell asleep.
choices.D: During the long boring, movie I fell asleep.

questions.explanation: The introductory phrase 'During the long, boring movie' ends with a comma before 'I fell asleep.'

questions.question: Which sentence is missing a needed comma?

choices.B: While we waited the rain stopped.
choices.C: After dinner, we washed the dishes.
choices.D: Well, that was surprising.

questions.explanation: 'While we waited' is an introductory clause and needs a comma: 'While we waited, the rain stopped.'

questions.question: Which sentence is correct as written?

choices.A: On Friday afternoon the class took a quiz.
choices.B: On Friday afternoon, the class took a quiz.
choices.C: On, Friday afternoon the class took a quiz.
choices.D: On Friday, afternoon the class took a quiz.

questions.explanation: The introductory phrase 'On Friday afternoon' should be followed by a single comma before the main clause.

questions.question: Why does 'After eating I felt better' need a comma?

choices.A: Because 'After eating' is an introductory phrase before the main idea.
choices.B: Because every sentence needs a comma.
choices.C: Because 'I' must always have a comma before it.
choices.D: It does not need a comma.

questions.explanation: The introductory phrase 'After eating' should be set off with a comma: 'After eating, I felt better.'

2-3.title: Commas with Joining Words (FANBOYS)
2-3.learn:
HOW TO USE A COMMA WITH FANBOYS

FANBOYS are the coordinating conjunctions: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. When one of these joins TWO complete sentences (two independent clauses), put a comma BEFORE it.

Example 1 — 'I wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.'
Both 'I wanted to swim' and 'the pool was closed' are complete sentences, so a comma goes before 'but.'

Example 2 — 'We studied hard, so we passed.'
Two complete sentences joined by 'so' need a comma before 'so.'

Example 3 — When NOT to use a comma: 'I wanted to swim but not dive.'
Here 'but not dive' is NOT a complete sentence, so NO comma is needed before 'but.'

Quick test: Cover the FANBOYS word and everything after it. If what's left AND what follows are both complete sentences, use a comma. If the part after the FANBOYS is not a full sentence, skip the comma.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a FANBOYS word?

choices.A: I like tea but I love coffee.
choices.B: I like tea, but I love coffee.
choices.C: I like tea but, I love coffee.
choices.D: I, like tea but I love coffee.

questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by 'but' need a comma before 'but.'

questions.question: Which word is a FANBOYS coordinating conjunction?

choices.B: although
choices.D: when

questions.explanation: 'So' is one of the FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). The others are subordinating conjunctions.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: She was tired, yet she finished the race.
choices.B: She was tired yet, she finished the race.
choices.C: She was tired yet she finished the race.
choices.D: She was, tired yet she finished the race.

questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by 'yet' take a comma before 'yet.'

questions.question: Which sentence does NOT need a comma before 'and'?

choices.A: I ran to the store, and I bought milk.
choices.B: I ran to the store and bought milk.
choices.C: The dog barked, and the cat hissed.
choices.D: We sang, and we danced.

questions.explanation: In choice B, 'bought milk' is not a complete sentence, so no comma is needed before 'and.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly joins two complete sentences with a comma + FANBOYS?

choices.A: We can walk or we can ride bikes.
choices.B: We can walk, or we can ride bikes.
choices.C: We can walk or, we can ride bikes.
choices.D: We, can walk or we can ride bikes.

questions.explanation: Both halves are complete sentences joined by 'or,' so a comma goes before 'or.'

questions.question: Where does the comma belong: 'The game was close so the fans were nervous'?

choices.A: The game was close, so the fans were nervous
choices.B: The game was, close so the fans were nervous
choices.C: The game was close so, the fans were nervous
choices.D: No comma is needed

questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by 'so' need a comma before 'so.'

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: He studied for hours, and aced the test.
choices.B: He studied for hours and aced the test.
choices.C: He studied, for hours and aced the test.
choices.D: He studied for hours and, aced the test.

questions.explanation: 'Aced the test' is not a complete sentence, so no comma is needed before 'and.'

questions.question: Which sentence needs a comma added before the FANBOYS word?

choices.B: She sings and dances.
choices.C: I wanted to go for I was bored.
choices.D: We read and we wrote together quietly.

questions.explanation: Choice C joins two complete sentences with 'for,' so it needs a comma: 'I wanted to go, for I was bored.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'nor' to join two complete sentences?

choices.A: He did not call, nor did he write.
choices.B: He did not call nor did he write.
choices.C: He did not call nor, did he write.
choices.D: He did, not call nor did he write.

questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by 'nor' need a comma before 'nor.'

questions.question: How do you decide whether to put a comma before 'but'?

choices.B: Use a comma only if BOTH parts are complete sentences.
choices.D: Put a comma after 'but,' not before it.

questions.explanation: A comma goes before a FANBOYS word only when it joins two complete sentences (independent clauses).

2-4.title: Colons & Semicolons
2-4.learn:
HOW TO USE COLONS AND SEMICOLONS

A SEMICOLON ( ; ) links two closely related COMPLETE sentences without a joining word: 'It was late; we went home.'
A COLON ( : ) introduces a list or an explanation AFTER a complete sentence: 'Bring three things: a pen, paper, and a calculator.'

Example 1 — Semicolon: 'I love summer; the days are long and warm.'
Both sides are complete sentences, closely related, so a semicolon joins them.

Example 2 — Colon before a list: 'Pack these items: sunscreen, a towel, and water.'
The part before the colon ('Pack these items') is a complete sentence, and the colon introduces the list.

Example 3 — Colon before an explanation: 'She had one goal: to win.'
The complete sentence 'She had one goal' is followed by a colon that explains what the goal was.

Rule of thumb: a colon needs a COMPLETE sentence in front of it. Never write 'Bring: a pen, paper' because 'Bring' alone is not a complete sentence.

questions.question: Which punctuation correctly joins two complete sentences: 'The rain stopped ___ the sun came out'?

choices.B: a colon (:)
choices.D: a hyphen (-)

questions.explanation: A semicolon links two closely related complete sentences without a joining word.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a colon to introduce a list?

choices.A: I packed: a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
choices.B: I packed three things; a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
choices.C: I packed three things: a hat, gloves, and a scarf.
choices.D: I: packed three things a hat gloves and a scarf.

questions.explanation: The complete sentence 'I packed three things' is followed by a colon that introduces the list.

questions.question: What kind of punctuation is a semicolon used for?

choices.B: To link two related complete sentences
choices.D: To end a question

questions.explanation: A semicolon links two closely related complete sentences without using a joining word.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

choices.A: We were hungry; so we ate.
choices.B: We were hungry; we ate lunch.
choices.C: We were; hungry we ate lunch.
choices.D: We were hungry; and we ate.

questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two complete sentences with no joining word; choices A and D wrongly add a conjunction.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a colon CORRECTLY?

choices.A: My favorite colors are: blue, green, and red.
choices.B: She wants: to travel the world.
choices.D: I have one rule: always be honest.

questions.explanation: A colon must follow a complete sentence; 'I have one rule' is complete, and the colon introduces the explanation.

questions.question: What is WRONG with 'For the trip bring: shoes, a jacket, and snacks'?

choices.B: The words before the colon ('For the trip bring') are not a complete sentence.
choices.D: Nothing is wrong.

questions.explanation: A colon must follow a complete sentence, but 'For the trip bring' is not complete on its own.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: The test was hard; many students struggled.
choices.B: The test was hard: many students struggled.
choices.C: The test was hard, many students struggled.
choices.D: The test, was hard many students struggled.

questions.explanation: Two closely related complete sentences are best joined with a semicolon.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a colon before an explanation?

choices.A: He knew the answer: the capital is Tallahassee.
choices.B: He knew: the answer the capital is Tallahassee.
choices.C: He knew the answer; the capital is Tallahassee:
choices.D: He knew the answer, the capital: is Tallahassee.

questions.explanation: The complete sentence 'He knew the answer' is followed by a colon that introduces the explanation.

questions.question: Which sentence should use a SEMICOLON, not a colon?

choices.A: Bring these tools ___ a hammer and nails.
choices.B: I finished my chores ___ now I can relax.
choices.C: She had one wish ___ to fly.
choices.D: Pack the basics ___ food and water.

questions.explanation: Choice B joins two complete sentences, which calls for a semicolon; the others introduce lists or explanations and use a colon.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.A: Remember one thing; practice makes perfect.
choices.B: Remember: one thing practice makes perfect.
choices.C: Remember one, thing practice makes perfect.
choices.D: Remember one thing: practice makes perfect.

questions.explanation: A colon follows the complete sentence 'Remember one thing' to introduce the explanation that follows.

2-5.title: Apostrophes: Contractions & Possessives
2-5.learn:
HOW TO USE APOSTROPHES

An apostrophe ( ' ) does two jobs:
1) POSSESSIVE — shows ownership: 'Maria's book' means the book belongs to Maria. Add 's to a singular noun. For a plural noun already ending in -s, just add an apostrophe: 'the students' lockers.'
2) CONTRACTION — marks where letters are dropped: 'do not' becomes 'don't,' and 'cannot' becomes 'can't.' The apostrophe stands in for the missing letters.

Example 1 — Possessive: 'The dog's bone.'
The bone belongs to the dog, so add 's to 'dog.'

Example 2 — Contraction: 'It is raining' becomes 'It's raining.'
The apostrophe replaces the missing 'i' in 'is.'

Example 3 — The tricky pair: 'its' vs 'it's.'
'Its' (no apostrophe) shows ownership: 'The cat licked its paw.'
'It's' (with apostrophe) ALWAYS means 'it is' or 'it has': 'It's cold today.'
Test: if you can replace it with 'it is,' use 'it's.' If not, use 'its.'

questions.question: Which word is the contraction for 'do not'?

choices.B: do'nt
choices.D: donot

questions.explanation: The apostrophe replaces the dropped 'o' in 'not,' making 'don't.'

questions.question: Which shows that the book belongs to Sam?

choices.B: Sam's book
choices.D: Sam book's

questions.explanation: To show one person owns something, add 's to the name: 'Sam's book.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The cat licked ___ paw.'

choices.B: its
choices.D: it is

questions.explanation: 'Its' (no apostrophe) shows ownership; the paw belongs to the cat.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: '___ going to rain today.'

choices.B: Its'
choices.D: Itss

questions.explanation: 'It's' means 'it is,' which fits here: 'It is going to rain today.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses the apostrophe CORRECTLY to show plural ownership?

choices.B: The students' lockers were clean.
choices.D: The students lockers' were clean.

questions.explanation: For a plural noun already ending in -s, add only an apostrophe: 'the students' lockers.'

questions.question: What does the apostrophe in 'they're' stand for?

choices.B: The missing letter in 'they are'
choices.D: Nothing — it is a mistake

questions.explanation: 'They're' is a contraction of 'they are,' and the apostrophe replaces the dropped 'a.'

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?

choices.B: The dog wagged its tail.
choices.D: The dog wagged it is tail.

questions.explanation: 'Its' shows ownership of the tail; 'it's' would wrongly mean 'it is.'

questions.question: Which sentence has an apostrophe error?

choices.B: The boys' team won the game.
choices.C: Its going to be a great day.
choices.D: We can't wait for summer.

questions.explanation: It should be 'It's going to be a great day' because 'it's' means 'it is.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence: ___

choices.A: Your the best friend Ive ever had.
choices.B: You're the best friend I've ever had.
choices.C: Youre the best friend Iv'e ever had.
choices.D: Your the best friend I've ever had.

questions.explanation: 'You're' means 'you are' and 'I've' means 'I have'; both contractions place the apostrophe where letters are dropped.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly shows ownership for a singular noun ending in -s, like 'the class'?

choices.B: the classes pet
choices.D: the class pet's

questions.explanation: For a singular noun, add 's to show ownership: 'the class's pet.'

2-6.title: Quotation Marks & Dialogue
2-6.learn:
HOW TO PUNCTUATE QUOTATIONS AND DIALOGUE

Put quotation marks ( " " ) around a speaker's EXACT words. Keep end punctuation (periods, commas, question marks) INSIDE the quotation marks. Use a comma to separate the spoken words from the speaker tag (like 'she said').

Example 1 — Tag first: She said, "Let's go."
A comma comes after 'said,' the quote starts with a capital letter, and the period sits inside the quotes.

Example 2 — Tag last: "I'm ready," he announced.
A comma (not a period) ends the quote inside the marks, then the tag 'he announced' follows.

Example 3 — Question inside a quote: "Are we there yet?" she asked.
The question mark stays inside the quotes, and the tag follows in lowercase.

Dialogue rule: start a NEW paragraph each time the speaker changes, so readers can follow who is talking.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.B: She said, "Hello."
choices.D: She said "Hello".

questions.explanation: A comma follows the tag 'She said,' the quote is capitalized, and the period sits inside the quotation marks.

questions.question: Where does the period go in a quotation?

choices.B: Outside the quotation marks
choices.C: There is no period in quotations
choices.D: Before the quotation marks open

questions.explanation: In American English, end punctuation like periods goes inside the quotation marks.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the quotation marks around the speaker's exact words?

choices.B: Tom yelled, Watch out!
choices.D: Tom "yelled, Watch out!"

questions.explanation: The exact words 'Watch out!' are inside quotation marks, with the exclamation point inside too.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quote that comes BEFORE the speaker tag?

choices.B: "I'm tired," she said.
choices.D: "I'm tired," She said.

questions.explanation: A comma replaces the period inside the quotes, and the tag 'she said' follows in lowercase.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a question inside a quote?

choices.B: "Where are you going?" he asked.
choices.D: Where are you going? he asked.

questions.explanation: The question mark stays inside the quotation marks, and the tag 'he asked' follows in lowercase.

questions.question: When should you start a NEW paragraph in dialogue?

choices.A: Every time a new sentence begins
choices.B: Each time the speaker changes
choices.C: Only at the end of the story
choices.D: Never — dialogue stays in one paragraph

questions.explanation: Starting a new paragraph each time the speaker changes helps readers follow the conversation.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

choices.B: "Let's eat". said Mom.
choices.D: Let's eat, said Mom.

questions.explanation: A comma ends the quote inside the marks, and the lowercase tag 'said Mom' follows.

questions.question: Which sentence has a punctuation ERROR?

choices.B: He whispered, "Be quiet."
choices.D: "Are you ready?" asked Dad.

questions.explanation: Choice C is missing the comma inside the quotes; it should read '"It's late," she said.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quote split by a tag in the middle?

choices.B: "I think" she said "we should leave."
choices.D: "I think," She said, "we should leave."

questions.explanation: Commas set off the tag 'she said,' the second part stays lowercase, and the period is inside the final quotes.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly capitalizes and punctuates the dialogue?

choices.B: The coach shouted, "Run faster!"
choices.D: The coach shouted, "run faster"!

questions.explanation: The sentence and the quote both start with capitals, a comma follows 'shouted,' and the exclamation point is inside the quotes.

2-7.title: Hyphens, Dashes & Ellipses
2-7.learn:
HOW TO USE HYPHENS, DASHES, AND ELLIPSES

HYPHEN ( - ) joins words into one idea, often before a noun: 'a well-known author,' 'a ten-year-old boy.' It connects words that work together as a single describer.
DASH ( — ) adds a dramatic pause or sets off extra information: 'I knew the answer — finally.'
ELLIPSIS ( ... ) shows a pause, a trailing-off, or that words were left out: 'I was going to say... never mind.'

Example 1 — Hyphen: 'a part-time job.'
'Part' and 'time' join with a hyphen to describe the job as one idea.

Example 2 — Dash: 'She finally won — after years of practice.'
The dash adds a dramatic pause before the extra detail.

Example 3 — Ellipsis: 'He opened the box and...'
The three dots show the sentence trailing off, building suspense.

Quick guide: hyphen = glue two words together; dash = a strong pause or break; ellipsis = a pause, trailing off, or missing words.

questions.question: Which mark joins two words into one idea, like 'well-known'?

choices.B: A dash
choices.D: A comma

questions.explanation: A hyphen joins words into a single idea, such as 'well-known author.'

questions.question: What does an ellipsis ( ... ) usually show?

choices.B: A pause or trailing off
choices.D: A strong command

questions.explanation: An ellipsis shows a pause, a trailing-off thought, or that words were left out.

questions.question: Which phrase correctly uses a hyphen?

choices.B: a ten-year-old boy
choices.D: a ten year-old boy

questions.explanation: When 'ten-year-old' describes the boy as one idea before the noun, all the words are hyphenated.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a dash for a dramatic pause?

choices.A: I finally finished my project — at midnight.
choices.B: I finally finished my project, at midnight.
choices.C: I finally finished my project... at midnight.
choices.D: I finally finished my-project at midnight.

questions.explanation: The dash adds a dramatic pause before the extra detail 'at midnight.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to show a trailing-off thought?

choices.A: I'm not sure, maybe we should.
choices.B: I'm not sure... maybe we should.
choices.D: I'm not sure; maybe we should.

questions.explanation: The ellipsis shows the speaker's thought trailing off before continuing.

questions.question: Which phrase needs a hyphen?

choices.B: a five star hotel
choices.D: a quiet room

questions.explanation: 'Five-star' should be hyphenated because the words join to describe the hotel as one idea.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a dash correctly to set off extra information?

choices.A: My best friend — Carla — moved away.
choices.B: My best friend-Carla-moved away.
choices.D: My best, friend Carla moved away.

questions.explanation: Dashes can set off extra information ('Carla') with a strong pause on each side.

questions.question: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?

choices.B: She is a self confident speaker.
choices.D: She is a self...confident speaker.

questions.explanation: 'Self-confident' is joined by a hyphen to work as one describing idea before 'speaker.'

questions.question: Which mark best fills the blank: 'We waited and waited ___ but no one came'?

choices.B: a dash, to add a dramatic pause
choices.D: a colon, to start a list

questions.explanation: A dash adds the dramatic pause that fits here: 'We waited and waited — but no one came.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses the ellipsis correctly?

choices.A: He started to speak... then stopped.
choices.B: He started to speak - then stopped.
choices.C: He started to speak, then, stopped.
choices.D: He started-to-speak then stopped.

questions.explanation: The ellipsis shows the pause as he starts to speak and then stops.
